verse.text: Simeon Peter, a slave and apostle of Jesus Christ, to those who have received a faith of equal standing with ours through the righteousness of our God and Savior Jesus Christ:
verse.note: The Greek has the Semitic spelling Symeōn rather than the usual ‘Simon’; it is used of Peter elsewhere only in Acts 15:14. Some manuscripts read the more familiar ‘Simon’, and many English versions print that form.

Most English versions have ‘servant’. The Greek word is the ordinary term for a slave, a person owned by a master, and a first-century reader would have heard it that way. In the Septuagint ‘slave of the Lord’ is also a title of honor for figures such as Moses, David and the prophets. Some recent translations likewise use ‘slave’.

note.term: our God and Savior Jesus Christ
note.traditional: of God and our Saviour Jesus Christ

verse.note: The Greek has a single article governing both nouns, the same construction as ‘our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ’ in verse 11. Most grammarians and modern translations therefore take it as calling Jesus both God and Savior. The alternative, ‘of our God and of the Savior Jesus Christ’, which distinguishes two persons as verse 2 does, is possible and is found in some older versions.

verse.text: May grace and peace be multiplied to you in the knowledge of God and of Jesus our Lord.
His divine power has given us everything needed for life and godliness, through the knowledge of the one who called us by his own glory and excellence.
verse.note: The Greek word is the standard term in Greek ethics for virtue or moral excellence, and was also used of a god’s displayed power and renown. The same word returns in verse 5 for a quality believers are to supply, and ‘excellence’ is used in both places so that the echo can be heard. Translations vary between ‘virtue’, ‘goodness’ and ‘excellence’, often using different words in the two verses.

verse.text: Through these he has given us the precious and very great promises, so that through them you may become sharers in the divine nature, having escaped the decay that is in the world because of desire.
verse.note: Traditionally ‘corruption’. The Greek word means perishing, decay or ruin, the opposite of the imperishability that belongs to the divine nature; in modern English ‘corruption’ chiefly suggests bribery or dishonesty. Moral ruin is included, since the decay is said to come through desire, and most translations keep ‘corruption’.

verse.text: For this very reason, make every effort to supply in your faith excellence, and in excellence knowledge,
and in knowledge self-control, and in self-control endurance, and in endurance godliness,
and in godliness brotherly affection, and in brotherly affection love.
For when these things are yours and are increasing, they keep you from being idle or unfruitful in the knowledge of our Lord Jesus Christ.
For whoever lacks these things is nearsighted to the point of blindness, having forgotten the cleansing of their former sins.
Therefore, brothers and sisters, put all the more effort into making your calling and election sure; for if you do these things you will never stumble.
For in this way the entrance into the eternal kingdom of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ will be richly supplied to you.
Therefore I intend always to remind you of these things, even though you know them and are firmly established in the truth that you have.
I consider it right, as long as I am in this tent, to rouse you with a reminder,

note.traditional: I think it meet; I think it right

verse.note: This word-family is normally rendered ‘righteous’ or ‘just’ in this translation. Here the adjective is used impersonally in a common idiom meaning that something is proper or fitting, so ‘right’ is used. Greek has one word-family where English divides between right/righteous and just/justice; ‘righteousness’ in verse 1 belongs to the same family.

Peter speaks of his body as a tent, a temporary shelter soon to be taken down; older versions have ‘tabernacle’ and some modern ones simply ‘body’. Paul uses similar imagery in 2 Corinthians 5:1–4. The word for ‘departure’ in verse 15 is exodos, the same word Luke uses for Jesus’s death in his account of the transfiguration (Luke 9:31).

verse.text: since I know that the putting off of my tent is coming soon, as indeed our Lord Jesus Christ made clear to me.
verse.note: The Greek adjective can mean ‘soon’ or ‘swift, sudden’, so the sense may be that Peter’s death is near or that it will come suddenly; most translations choose ‘soon’. What Jesus ‘made clear’ is usually connected with the saying about Peter’s death in John 21:18–19, though the letter does not say so.

verse.text: And I will make every effort so that after my departure you will be able at any time to call these things to mind.
For we were not following cleverly devised myths when we made known to you the power and coming of our Lord Jesus Christ; on the contrary, we had been eyewitnesses of his majesty.
verse.note: The Greek word was used for the arrival and presence of a ruler or dignitary on an official visit, and among early Christians for the future arrival of Jesus in glory. Most interpreters take it that way here, with the transfiguration described in the next verses offered as a preview that guarantees it. A minority think the reference is to his first coming.

verse.text: For he received honor and glory from God the Father when a voice such as this was borne to him by the Majestic Glory: “This is my Son, my beloved, in whom I delight.”

note.traditional: came (of the voice and of prophecy); moved or carried along (of the prophets)

verse.note: The same Greek verb, ‘carry’ or ‘bear’, is used four times in this passage: of the voice in verses 17 and 18, and in verse 21 of prophecy and of the prophets. Most translations vary the English, which hides the link drawn between the voice from heaven and the prophetic word. ‘Borne’ is used each time here to keep it.

verse.text: We ourselves heard this voice borne from heaven when we were with him on the holy mountain.
So we have the prophetic word made all the more sure, and you do well to pay attention to it as to a lamp shining in a murky place, until the day dawns and the morning star rises in your hearts.

note.traditional: a more sure word of prophecy

verse.note: The Greek says literally ‘we have the prophetic word more sure’. This can mean that the prophetic word has been confirmed by what the apostles saw on the mountain, as rendered here and in many modern translations. It can also mean that the prophetic word is something even more sure than that experience, as in the older tradition. Some take the comparative simply as ‘altogether reliable’.

verse.text: Know this first of all: no prophecy of Scripture comes about by anyone’s own interpretation,
verse.note: The Greek is terse: literally, no prophecy of Scripture ‘comes to be of one’s own interpretation’. The rendering here takes this of the prophecy’s origin: it did not arise from the prophet’s own reading of events, which fits the explanation in verse 21. The other long-standing reading applies it to the reader: no prophecy is a matter for private interpretation. Scholars are divided.

verse.text: for no prophecy was ever borne by human will; rather, human beings, borne along by the Holy Spirit, spoke from God.

But false prophets also arose among the people, just as there will be false teachers among you too. They will smuggle in destructive teachings, even denying the Master who bought them, and so bring swift destruction on themselves.
verse.note: The Greek word meant a chosen school of thought, a party, or its distinctive views; it was used neutrally of philosophical schools and of Jewish groups such as the Pharisees. 'Heresy' in the later sense of doctrine condemned by church authority is an anachronism here, though this verse is one of the places where the word is moving in a negative direction. Some scholars prefer 'factions' or 'sects'; most translations keep 'heresies'.

The word is the ordinary term for the owner of slaves, not the usual word for 'Lord'. The picture is of a slave purchased by a new owner and then disowning him; the 'Master' is generally taken to be Christ.

verse.text: Many will follow them in their debauchery, and because of them the way of truth will be slandered.
verse.note: The Greek verb means to speak abusively or defame, whether the object is God, people, or things. English 'blaspheme' is now limited to speech against God, which does not fit its uses in this chapter (the way of truth, the glorious ones, things not understood). The same word-family is rendered 'slander' and 'slanderous' in verses 10–12.

verse.text: In their greed they will exploit you with fabricated words. For a long time now their condemnation has not been idle, and their destruction is not asleep.
For if God did not spare angels when they sinned, but consigned them to Tartarus in chains of gloom and handed them over to be kept for judgment;
verse.note: The Greek is a single verb, 'to send to Tartarus', found only here in the New Testament. In Greek tradition Tartarus was the deep prison below Hades where the defeated Titans were held, and Jewish writers in Greek had adopted the name for the place where rebel angels are confined. 'Hell' blurs this with other terms; here it is a place of detention before judgment, not the final punishment. The story assumed is the Jewish tradition, built on Genesis 6:1–4, of angels who sinned before the flood.

Manuscripts are divided between two similar-looking words: 'chains' (seirais) and 'pits' (sirois). Several important early manuscripts read 'pits of gloom'; the edition translated here reads 'chains', which also matches the parallel in Jude 6. Either reading yields the same picture of imprisonment in darkness.

verse.text: and if he did not spare the ancient world, but protected Noah, a herald of righteousness, with seven others, when he brought a flood on the world of the ungodly;
and if he condemned the cities of Sodom and Gomorrah to ruin, reducing them to ashes, and made them an example of what is coming for the ungodly;
and if he rescued righteous Lot, who was worn down by the debauched conduct of unprincipled people—
for by what he saw and heard while living among them, that righteous man tormented his righteous soul day after day over their lawless deeds—
then the Lord knows how to rescue the godly from trial, and how to keep the unrighteous under punishment for the day of judgment,
verse.note: The Greek participle is present tense and most naturally means the unrighteous are already being punished while they are held for the day of judgment. Some scholars and translations take it with a future sense: 'to keep the unrighteous to be punished at the day of judgment'. The grammar allows either.

verse.text: especially those who go after the flesh in defiling desire and despise authority. Brazen and arrogant, they do not tremble as they slander the glorious ones,
verse.note: Literally 'glories'. Most scholars take this as a term for angelic beings, as in the parallel at Jude 8, though whether good angels or fallen ones are meant is disputed; verse 11 may suggest the latter, since even angels do not denounce 'them'. Older translations understood human or church authorities ('dignities').

verse.text: whereas angels, though greater in strength and power, do not bring a slanderous judgment against them.
verse.note: Many manuscripts add 'before the Lord' after these words, and some read 'from the Lord'; others have neither phrase. The edition translated here follows the shorter text, while many translations include 'before the Lord'. 'Them' most likely refers to the glorious ones of verse 10.

verse.text: But these people, like unreasoning animals, creatures of instinct born to be caught and destroyed, slander what they do not understand, and in the destruction of those creatures they too will be destroyed,

note.term: in the destruction of those creatures
note.traditional: shall utterly perish in their own corruption

verse.note: The Greek says 'in their destruction they too will be destroyed', and 'their' could refer either to the animals just mentioned or to the false teachers themselves. The rendering takes it of the animals: the teachers will meet the same end as the beasts they resemble. The same Greek word is rendered 'corruption' in verse 19, where moral decay is in view; the older tradition used 'corruption' here as well.

verse.text: suffering wrong as the wages of wrongdoing. They count reveling in the daytime a pleasure. They are stains and blemishes, reveling in their deceptions as they feast with you.

note.term: suffering wrong as the wages of wrongdoing
note.traditional: and shall receive the reward of unrighteousness

verse.note: The reading followed here is a deliberate play on words: those who did wrong are 'wronged' in return, that is, paid back in harm. The expression is harsh, and many manuscripts have the smoother 'receiving the wages of wrongdoing'. Some interpreters take the harder reading to mean 'cheated of the wages of wrongdoing'.

Some manuscripts read 'their love feasts' (agapais) instead of 'their deceptions' (apatais), a difference of two letters in Greek. 'Love feasts' matches the parallel in Jude 12 and may have been copied from there. The mention of feasting together shows that the community's shared meals are in view in either case.

verse.text: They have eyes full of adultery that never rest from sin; they lure unstable souls; they have hearts trained in greed. Children of a curse!
Leaving the straight way, they have gone astray and followed the way of Balaam son of Bosor, who loved the wages of wrongdoing

note.traditional: Balaam the son of Bosor / Beor

verse.note: In Numbers 22–24 Balaam's father is called Beor, and a few manuscripts correct the name to that form here. 'Bosor' is the better-attested reading; why the author used it is uncertain, and one suggestion is a play on the Hebrew word for 'flesh'. Balaam was the prophet hired to curse Israel, whose donkey spoke to stop him; later Jewish tradition treated him as the type of a teacher corrupted by money.

verse.text: but was rebuked for his own lawbreaking: a voiceless donkey, speaking in a human voice, restrained the prophet’s madness.
These people are waterless springs and mists driven by a storm; for them the gloom of darkness has been kept.
For, speaking swollen words of emptiness, they lure with the desires of the flesh, with debauchery, those who are barely escaping from people who live in error,
promising them freedom while they themselves are slaves of corruption; for people are enslaved to whatever has overcome them.

For if, having escaped the defilements of the world through knowledge of the Lord and Savior Jesus Christ, they are again entangled in them and overcome, their last state has become worse than their first.
For it would have been better for them not to have known the way of righteousness than, having known it, to turn back from the holy commandment handed on to them.
What the true proverb says has happened to them: “A dog goes back to its own vomit,” and, “A sow, once washed, goes back to wallowing in the mud.”
verse.note: The first saying corresponds to Proverbs 26:11, though not in the wording of the Greek Old Testament. The second is not from Scripture; similar sayings about a washed pig returning to the mud circulated in ancient wisdom literature, including versions of the story of Ahiqar. Dogs and pigs were both regarded as unclean animals.

verse.text: This, dear friends, is now the second letter I am writing to you. In both of them I am stirring up your sincere minds by way of reminder,
so that you remember the words spoken beforehand by the holy prophets and the command of the Lord and Savior given through your apostles.
Know this first of all: in the last days scoffers will come with their scoffing, following their own desires
and saying, “Where is the promise of his coming? For ever since the fathers fell asleep, everything goes on just as it has from the beginning of creation.”
verse.note: The Greek word means arrival and presence, and in this period was regularly used for the official visit of a ruler to a city. Early Christians used it for the expected arrival of Jesus as Lord and judge. The scoffers' point is that this promised arrival has not happened.

This may mean Israel's ancestors, which is the usual sense of 'the fathers' in the New Testament, or the first generation of Christians, who were expected to see the Lord's coming and have now died. Scholars are divided. 'Fell asleep' is the common early Christian way of speaking of death.

verse.text: For they deliberately let this escape them: that long ago there were heavens, and an earth formed out of water and through water by the word of God,
verse.note: Throughout this chapter the Greek is plural and refers to the created heavens paired with the earth, not specifically to God's dwelling or simply to the visible sky. The plural 'heavens' is therefore kept in every occurrence, echoing 'the heavens and the earth' of Genesis; this is also the traditional rendering here.

note.term: they deliberately let this escape them

verse.note: The Greek can also be read 'in maintaining this, it escapes them that...', taking 'this' as the scoffers' claim in verse 4. The rendering chosen, in which their ignorance is willful, is the majority view. The same verb 'escape' returns in verse 8, where the readers are told not to let a different fact escape them.

verse.text: and through these the world of that time was deluged with water and perished.
verse.note: The Greek pronoun is plural and its reference is uncertain. It most likely points to the water and the word of God together, or to the two mentions of water in verse 5; some take it to refer to the heavens. In any case, the same means by which the world was formed served to destroy it in the flood.

verse.text: But the present heavens and earth have been stored up by the same word for fire, kept for the day of judgment and destruction of ungodly people.
But do not let this one thing escape you, dear friends: with the Lord one day is like a thousand years, and a thousand years like one day.

note.term: one day is like a thousand years

verse.note: This echoes Psalm 90:4, 'a thousand years in your sight are like yesterday when it has passed.' The point is not a formula for calculating dates. God does not measure delay on a human scale.

verse.text: The Lord is not slow to keep his promise, as some count slowness, but is patient toward you, not wanting any to perish but all to come to turning back.
verse.note: The traditional 'repentance' now suggests mainly feeling sorry. The Greek word, shaped by the prophets' call to 'return' to God, means a change of direction in mind and conduct. Most translations keep 'repentance' as an established term understood to include a changed life.

verse.text: But the day of the Lord will come like a thief. On that day the heavens will pass away with a roar, the elements will be dissolved in burning heat, and the earth and the works done on it will be found out.
verse.note: The word can mean the basic substances of the physical world (earth, air, fire, water), the heavenly bodies (sun, moon and stars), or, less likely here, spiritual powers. Standing between 'the heavens' and 'the earth', it may well mean the heavenly bodies, but the general term 'elements' leaves the question open, as the Greek does.

The oldest manuscripts read 'will be found', which SBLGNT and most modern editions adopt. Many later manuscripts read 'will be burned up', and there are other variants, probably because scribes found the original puzzling. The likely sense is that the earth and all that has been done on it will be exposed to God's judgment; the same verb returns in verse 14, 'to be found by him spotless'. The meaning remains disputed.

verse.text: Since all these things are to be dissolved in this way, what kind of people you ought to be in holy conduct and godliness,
waiting for and hastening the coming of the day of God, because of which the heavens will be set on fire and dissolved, and the elements will melt in burning heat!
verse.note: The verb can mean 'hasten, speed up' or 'be eager for, strive toward'. With a direct object, as here, 'hasten' is the more natural sense, and it fits a Jewish idea that the turning back of God's people can bring the day nearer (compare verse 9). Some translations prefer 'eagerly desiring'.

verse.text: But in keeping with his promise we are waiting for new heavens and a new earth, where righteousness has its home.
Therefore, dear friends, since you are waiting for these things, make every effort to be found by him spotless and blameless, in peace,
and count our Lord’s patience as salvation, just as our dear brother Paul also wrote to you, according to the wisdom given to him,

as he does in all his letters too, when he speaks in them about these things. In them are some things hard to understand, which the untaught and unstable twist, as they do the rest of the Scriptures, to their own destruction.
verse.note: The Greek word means 'writings', but in the New Testament it regularly refers to the sacred Scriptures. The phrase 'the rest of' places Paul's letters alongside them, one of the earliest signs that his letters were being read as authoritative writings.

verse.text: You, then, dear friends, knowing this in advance, be on your guard, so that you are not carried away by the error of the lawless and fall from your own stability.
But grow in the grace and knowledge of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ. To him be the glory both now and to the day of eternity. Amen.
verse.note: The Greek is literally 'to the day of the age', an unusual phrase where 'to the ages' would be expected. It may mean the day that begins the age to come, the 'day of God' of verse 12, or the endless day that is eternity itself. The rendering keeps the image of a day, which most traditional translations smooth to 'for ever'.
